pages.text: T. rex had lips, upending its enduring pop culture image | National Geographic Premium SCIENCE ​ T. rex had lips, upending its enduring pop culture image Whether carnivorous dinosaurs had lips has long been the stuff of paleo-debate. A new study finds evidence that flesh covered the predators’ teeth. Tyrannosaurus rex and other carnivorous dinosaurs likely had soft tissue that covered their sharp teeth, as seen in this illustration. Lips would have kept their teeth moist and protected—and ready to attack prey. Illustration by Mark P. Witton By Riley Black Published March 30, 2023 • 6 min read The fearsome jaws of Tyrannosaurus are famous. In museum halls, paleo art, and even feature films such as Jurassic Park , the Cretaceous carnivore has traditionally been depicted with banana-size fangs and a sinister grin. But paleontologists have now discovered that the living animal did not have a sharp-toothed smirk— T. rex , as well as many other carnivorous dinosaurs, had lips. Reported today in Science , a multi-institution team of paleontologists propose that carnivorous dinosaurs like T. rex and Allosaurus had fleshy lips covering their teeth, much as modern-day lizards do. The hypothesis will likely alter both the public image of dinosaurs as well as how paleontologists study the ways these terrible lizards fed. pages.description: The formidable Tyrannosaurus rex had nothing to fear—except possibly its own kind, gnawed fossil bones suggest.
pages.text: T. Rex Was a Cannibal, Bone Gashes Suggest | National Geographic Tooth gouges on this 65-million-year-old T. rex toe bone could have been made only by another T. rex. Diagram courtesy Nicholas Longrich, Yale University T. Rex Was a Cannibal, Bone Gashes Suggest Mighty predators may have attacked kin or scavenged corpses. By Brian Handwerk Published October 15, 2010 • 3 min read The formidable Tyrannosaurus rex likely had nothing to fear—except possibly its own kind, a new study suggests. Paleontologist Nick Longrich of Yale University was examining dinosaur bones found in Montana when he noticed large gouges in bones that had yet to be indentifiied. The gouges had to have been made by a large carnivore, he said, and when the mystery fossils were deposited 65 million years ago, T. rex was the only North American carnivore large and toothy enough to make such marks. But the seemingly routine find took a macabre turn when Longrich discovered one of the bitten bones belonged to a T. rex —making it apparent evidence of cannibalism. This toe bone "has giant theropod bite marks, and the only one there [at that time] was T. rex ," he said. "There was really no other conclusion I could come to." (Related: "Tiny T. rex Ancestors Achieved World Domination." ) Further analysis in several fossil collections turned up three more similarly bitten T. rex bones. Longrich and colleagues speculate the giant predators may have engaged in cannibalism with some regularity—but it's unknown whether the dinosaurs fought to the death or simply scavenged T. rex corpses. Employers use Form 8850 to prescreen and to make a written request to the state workforce agency of the state in which their business is located (where the employee works) to certify an individual as a member of a targeted group for purposes of qualifying for the work opportunity credit. Disabled Access Credit — The Disabled Access Credit provides a non-refundable credit of up to $5,000 for small businesses that incur expenditures for the purpose of providing access to persons with disabilities. An eligible small business is one that earned $1 million or less or had no more than 30 full time employees in the previous year; they may take the credit each and every year they incur access expenditures. pages.text: The 11 most astonishing scientific discoveries of 2023 | National Geographic By Dina Fine Maron Published December 6, 2023 • 12 min read In another stellar year for science, astronomers unveiled new discoveres about the cosmos, biologists etched out a clearer map of our planet’s creatures, and paleontologists painted a richer picture of the dinosaurs that roamed Earth millions of years ago. The latest compendium of humanity’s scientific research continues to intrigue and reveal new mysteries to solve. Here are some of National Geographic ’s top picks for 2023’s most fascinating breakthroughs. 1. Astronomers detect immense ripples in the fabric of space-time For the first time, scientists detected low-frequency gravitational waves moving through the galaxy. These cosmic ripples are likely the distant echoes of supermassive black holes interacting and merging many billions of light-years away. A consortium of international researchers discovered these cosmic waves by measuring tiny time variations in radio signals from pulsar stars. The findings suggest that there were far more behemoth black holes in the early universe than previously thought, and continuing to study this new type of gravitational wave could help unravel details about the origins of our universe and better explain the unseen substances and forces that power the cosmos. 2. Learn about other national symbols. History of the American flag The flag of the United States is a symbol of freedom before which Americans recite the pledge of allegiance . The flag's 13 red and white stripes represent the 13 original colonies. Its 50 white stars on a blue background represent the 50 states. Each of the colors on the flag has a meaning: Red: valor and bravery White: purity and innocence Blue: vigilance, perseverance, and justice A star is added to the flag when a new state joins the United States. The flag was last modified on July 4, 1960, when Hawaii was incorporated as a state. Learn more about the evolution of the American flag and its earlier designs. How to raise the flag Follow these guidelines to properly display the American flag [PDF, 162KB]. When to fly the flag at half-staff The American flag flies at half-staff or at half-mast when the country or a state is in mourning. The president, a state governor, or the mayor of the District of Columbia can order flags to fly at half-staff. In most cases, an American flag flying at half-staff marks one of three observances: The death of a government official, military member, or emergency first responder A national tragedy Memorial Day or another national day of remembrance The Great Seal The Great Seal of the United States is a national symbol used in official documents such as treaties and commissions. PETER BREUNIG By Carlos Micó Published July 27, 2026 In 1886, when Nigeria was a colony of the British Empire, the Royal Niger Company gained exclusive mineral rights over the Jos Plateau in central Nigeria, an area rich in tin ore and inhabited by the Berom people. In the foothills, access routes to the mines ran through an area called Nok. Over the years, with the exploitation of the mines and the local people who overwhelmingly provided the labor force, numerous fragments of ancient pottery came to light but were largely ignored. One piece, too striking to be disregarded, appeared in 1928: a small monkey head, sculpted in terra-cotta. The mine manager, Lt. Col. John Dent Young, had that piece and other fragments transferred to a museum in the city of Jos, the provincial capital. Fifteen years later, a miner found another terra-cotta head and took it home, where he used it as a scarecrow, apparently with some success. A British engineer noticed the piece about a year later, and brought it to Jos, where he showed it to Bernard Fagg, an archaeologist working in Nigeria as a civil administrator for the British Colonial Service. pages.text: The Ancient Princess Who Crushed Enemies With Her Quick Tongue | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The Ancient Princess Who Crushed Enemies With Her Quick Tongue Priestess of the moon god and daughter of Sargon the Great, Enheduanna amassed political power and waged war with her honeyed words. Enheduanna is often identified as the first author who appears independently in the historical record. Her hymns to the gods of Akkad and Sumer survived centuries after her death—and their translations are changing what modern scholars know about the role of women in the ancient Middle East. Photo Illustration, NGM Staff. Source Photo for Illustration: Yale Peabody Museum By Liddy Berman Published September 8, 2026 More than 4,000 years ago, Enheduanna, high priestess of the Sumerian moon god and daughter of a king, labored over a palm-size clay tablet. Reed stylus in her hand, she pressed its tiny wedge-shaped tip into the clay to build the small, spiky characters of cuneiform. She had been driven from her temple home by a rebel leader who opposed her family’s imperial rule over the kingdoms of Ur and Uruk. Though exiled and frightened, she was far from powerless—her words were believed to influence the gods. In her writings, Enheduanna petitioned her patron goddess— Inanna , the Mesopotamian deity of love, war and change—to rescue her from the dark fate awaiting political exiles and restore her to her rightful position as high priestess. pages.text: The Artisans Trying to Bring Back Neolithic Fashion | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The Artisans Trying to Bring Back Neolithic Fashion A growing community of craftspeople are trying to build knowledge of ancient clothing—by making it themselves. Historical craft specialist Vasi Birchwood recreates fashion from the Neolithic period on her Youtube channel. This outfit is one of her creations. The jacket is made of deer skin, stitched with deer skin cord and a bone awl, and adorned with moose teeth. The shirt underneath the jacket is made of undyed linen, hand stitched with linen thread. The skirt is made of deer skin and decorated with braided hemp strings. Photo Illustration: NGM Staff; Source Photos for Illustration: Vasi Birchwood By Starre Vartan Published November 2, 2026 Around the fire, no one seems especially bothered by the rain. Some people duck beneath bark shelters to continue twisting cordage from plant fibers. Others cook foraged plants or work leather while steam rises from damp clothing. A few wander into the drizzle to gather more wood before returning to the warmth of the flames. Among them is historical craft specialist and YouTube educator Vasi Birchwood . For Birchwood, weather isn't an inconvenience so much as another participant in this meeting of experiential archeologists and craft experts in Northern Germany. pages.text: The Complicated Social Life of a Tyrannosaurus Rex | National Geographic SCIENCE Why Everything We Thought We Knew About T. Rex is Getting … Messier Fossil evidence has shifted our view of T. rex from a complete loner tyrant into a more nuanced carnivore. Scarred skulls, scraped ground, and fossilized trackways suggest adult tyrannosaurs lived largely solitary lives, like modern big cats, but also gathered in communal display arenas to woo potential mates. GERD LUDWIG, National Geographic Image Collection By Riley Black Published October 8, 2026 Every time I’m in New York, I have to visit her. She’s always waiting in the same place, standing on the fourth floor of the American Museum of Natural History, grinning so wide that her teeth gleam under the bright lights. Experts know her as AMNH 5027. I know her as the first T yrannosaurus rex I ever met. Before the discovery of “Sue,” “Stan,” “Scotty,” and many other famous skeletons of Earth’s last great carnivorous dinosaur, AMNH 5027 was the icon. The partial skeleton was the first T . rex to include a complete skull – only slightly smushed. It left no doubt that the dinosaur was an impressive flesh-ripper, reconstructed with jaws agape when the museum’s paleontologists assembled real bones and casts in the world’s first great introduction to the dinosaur. (And, when Michael Crichton’s Jurassic Park needed a skeletal dinosaur for the cover, AMNH 5027 was the model.) pages.description: Paleontologists are resurrecting a famous Egyptian fossil site after a World War II air raid obliterated its most spectacular dinosaur discoveries—and their findings reveal a world even deadlier than expected.
pages.text: The Dinosaurs That Went Extinct ... Twice | National Geographic By Nicholas St. Fleur Published August 14, 2026 Stones & Bones is back! I’m Nicholas St. Fleur, a science editor at National Geographic, and today we explore the “lost dinosaurs” of the Bahariya Oasis in Egypt. Want to make sure you get every Stones & Bones newsletter? Enter your email here . To Egyptologists, the Bahariya Oasis is known as the Valley of Golden Mummies, a necropolis where archaeologists have uncovered hundreds of gilded and decorated mummies dating back to the Greco-Roman era, roughly 2,000 years ago. But to paleontologists, the oasis is sacred because of something far older and far more legendary: Spinosaurus . The first ever specimen of this ferocious river monster was collected here more than a hundred years ago, along with fossils of several other enigmatic dinosaurs. Until they were lost forever, casualties of the World War II bombing that destroyed much of Munich. Swallowed by the flames, these dinosaurs essentially went extinct twice. National Geographic Explorer Hesham Sallam , a paleontologist at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center in Egypt, has spent the past decade collecting clues to what the Bahariya Oasis looked like nearly 100 million years ago, long before it was buried beneath the desert. His team is still working to rebuild what was lost when the bombs obliterated the collection. pages.text: The Echoes of Toothed Birds | National Geographic Photo by Brian Switek. SCIENCE LAELAPS The Echoes of Toothed Birds By Riley Black Published May 22, 2015 • 4 min read Whenever I spot a grebe, I try to imagine the bird with teeth. This is another symptom of a chronically fossiliferous mind. You see, these snake-necked swimming birds have traditionally been taken as a proxy for a specific sort of ancient avian called hesperornithiforms. Best known by, as you might guess, Hesperornis – these toothed birds pioneered the diving lifestyle between 113 and 66 million years ago. Today’s grebes and loons look like edentulous echos of these lost Cretaceous days, or, as beautifully expressed by ornithologist William Beebe : When in the depth of the winter, a full hundred miles from the nearest land, one sees a loon in the path of the steamer, listens to its weird, maniacal laughter, and sees it slowly sink downward through the green waters, it truly seems a hint of the bird-life of long-past ages. No surprise, then, that paleontologists past sometimes considered loons and grebes to be the descendants of Hesperornis . Their bones carry the same superficial similarity. But this is an evolutionary ruse known as convergence. Loons and grebes are copycats that independently took up the same lifestyle as the toothed birds that dove after fish in warm Cretaceous seas and sometimes wound up in the stomachs of monstrous marine reptiles. pages.text: The federal budget process | USAGov Skip to main content The federal budget process Learn about the federal government’s budget process. Steps include the president creating the budget plan and Congress’s work creating funding bills for the president to sign. Annual funding areas Every year, the U.S. Congress begins work on a federal budget for the next fiscal year. The federal government’s fiscal year runs from October 1 of one calendar year through September 30 of the next. And the annual budget covers three spending areas: Mandatory spending - funding for Social Security, Medicare, veterans benefits, and other spending required by law. This typically uses over half of all funding. Discretionary spending - federal agency funding. Congress sets funding levels for these each year. This usually accounts for around a third of all funding. Interest on the debt - this usually uses less than 10 percent of all funding. Creating the U.S. federal budget The budget planning begins a year before the budget is to go into effect. Federal agencies create budget requests and submit them to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB). OMB refers to the agencies’ requests as it develops the budget proposal for the president. The president submits the budget proposal to Congress early the next year. Proposed funding is divided among 12 subcommittees, which hold hearings. Each handles funding for different government functions such as defense spending or energy and water. pages.text: The Little Ice Age was brutal. How did people survive? | National Geographic During the Little Ice Age, the Northern Hemisphere experienced long stretches of temperatures so cold that crops failed and rivers froze—like the Scheldt River, depicted here outside of Antwerp, Belgium, in a 1593 oil painting by Lucas van Valckenborch. Photograph by incamerastock, Alamy Stock Photo Premium ENVIRONMENT The Little Ice Age was brutal. How did people survive? From roughly the 16th to 19th centuries, much of the Earth was gripped by a persistent frigid cold. It left ripples through history—and some lessons for today’s climate crisis. By Kieran Mulvaney Published February 20, 2024 Thousands of people walking and playing across the frozen River Thames. Soldiers on horseback capturing ships stuck in the ice. Indigenous populations using snowshoes to outfox English interlopers. Accused witches put on trial as their communities struggled to explain crop failures and extreme cold. These were some of the images that define the Little Ice Age—a period of several centuries last millennium in which parts of the Northern Hemisphere grappled with a persistent cold. But what caused the Little Ice Age, how long did it last, how did people adapt to its frigid grip—and what lessons can we learn as we enter our own period of climatic change? ( Broken Baculum a Sign of Painful Ice Age Injury) What is the Little Ice Age—and what caused it? The Little Ice Age was not a true ice age—average cooling was probably only in the order of 0.5 degrees Celsius , or 1 degree Fahrenheit—nor was it consistently cold.

pages.text: The most audacious thefts at the Louvre in the last century | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The Louvre has a wild history of being robbed in broad daylight One of the most infamous heists in the cultural institution’s history was the 1911 theft of the Mona Lisa—when Pablo Picasso numbered among the suspects. People gather around the Mona Lisa painting in Paris, three years after it was stolen from the Louvre by Vincenzo Peruggia in 1911. The theft is one of the most famous in the museum's history. Roger-Viollet, Getty Images By Erin Blakemore Published October 19, 2025 It took just seven minutes for a group of audacious thieves to pull off what may have been one of the most daring crimes in modern art: the theft of Napoleonic-era jewels from the Louvre in Paris on the morning of October 19. The heist, which took place while the museum was open to the public, involved a variety of jewels once owned by members of the French monarchy, including an emerald necklace and earrings that Napoleon gave his second wife Marie-Louise for their wedding. Now, questions are raging about how masked men could successfully evade security and nab priceless objets d’art from one of the most important art institutions in the world. It’s far from the first time. The museum has a longstanding history of shocking break-ins and unsolved thefts—despite being built precisely to protect the nation’s cultural heritage in the wake of a bloody revolution. But its monsters and magic may have been based on real science. Odysseus faced the cyclops, his men turned into pigs, and he sailed between a six-headed monster and a whirlpool. Each of these, it turns out, have potential real-life explanations. In Homer's epic poem, Odysseus blinded the cyclops Polyphemus. Researchers have suggested that ancient people might have encountered fossils that could have resembled a giant, one-eyed creature. Alfredo Dagli Orti, Art Resource, NY By Bethany Brookshire Published July 17, 2026 The Odyssey is a myth. It’s doubtful that a man took a literal decade to make it from Troy on the coast of modern-day Turkey to the Greek island of Ithaca after the Trojan War, cursed to make love to witches, journey to Hades, and pick fights with a cyclops. Or at least, if he did take that long, his curse probably involved not asking for directions. But the tale of Odysseus’ extra-long journey home contains hints of things that people might have encountered in the ancient world, from a real-life cyclops to killer whirlpools and hallucinogenic plants. As Matt Damon steps into the famous wanderer’s sandals in The Odyssey on July 17, here are some of the scientific realities behind his legendary side quests. pages.text: The Political Turmoil Behind Goya’s Black Paintings | National Geographic HISTORY & CULTURE The Political Turmoil Behind Goya’s Black Paintings After the expulsion of Napoleon’s forces, and with Spain under absolutist rule again, Francisco de Goya poured his existential pessimism into works known as the Black Paintings. The Black Paintings Titled “Atropos” (“The Fates”), this work by Francisco de Goya shows a man bound at the mercy of the three Fates, or Moirai, the goddesses of Greek mythology who spun the thread of destiny, measured and allotted it, and cut it short. Atropos was the name of the cutter. Oronoz/Album By José Antonio Vigara Zafra Published November 2, 2026 At the outbreak of the Peninsular War (also known as the War of Spanish Independence) in 1808, Francisco de Goya was already one of Spain’s most esteemed and sought-after artists. After settling in Madrid in 1775, at the age of 29, the painter did not take long to close in on the crown—first, painting designs for the tapestries destined to adorn the royal palaces, and later, working as a portraitist to the country’s aristocratic elite. A portrait of Francisco de Goya from 1826, at 80 years old, by Vicente López Portaña. DEA/Album In 1789, Goya was appointed court painter, and later reached the height of his official career as first court painter to King Charles IV in 1799. pages.text: The Treasures Emerging From Turkey’s Dying Lakes | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The Treasures Emerging From Turkey’s Dying Lakes Climate change is exposing once-submerged churches, castles and petroglyphs—and threatening their survival. The Basilica of Saint Neophytos, the likely site of early Christianity's Nicene Council, used to be submerged beneath Lake İznik. But drought has caused the lake's waters to recede, exposing the ancient structure. Sercan Ozkurnazl, Getty Images By Katie Nadworny Published September 24, 2026 Mustafa Şahin used to spend much more of his time below water. As the founder of Turkey’s first underwater archaeology department, he practiced his work in the country’s lakes, diving deep to uncover important historical ruins. In 2014, he found the Basilica of Saint Neophytos—a contender for the home of the original Nicene Council —in Lake İznik, a discovery that Archaeology Magazine and The Archaeological Institute of America deemed one of the most important that year. But Mustafa isn’t diving anymore. His work as head archaeologist of the basilica now keeps him out of the lake, because Saint Neophytos is no longer under İznik’s waters. It sits on dry ground. Lake İznik is facing a crisis and it isn’t alone. Turkey is losing most of its lakes at an alarming rate: close to 75 percent are in the process of disappearing, many within the last decade. pages.text: This bizarre new dinosaur has something in common with modern sloths | National Geographic SCIENCE This bizarre new dinosaur has something in common with modern sloths Like T. rex and some modern sloths, this strange 90 million year old dinosaur had two fingers on each hand. An illustration shows what Duonychus tsogtbaatari might have looked like. Unlike its therizinosaur brethren, the new species had only two claws instead of three. Illustration by Masato Hattori By Riley Black Published March 25, 2025 Therizinosaurs were some of the strangest dinosaurs of all time. Descended from carnivores , the prehistoric reptiles were plant-eaters and had fuzzy feathered bodies, small heads with peg-like teeth in their jaws, bulbous stomachs that acted like fermenting vats for heaps of vegetation, and impressively large claws on each of their hands. Their build and claws have drawn comparisons to sloths, but some of these reptiles stood over 13 feet tall and weighed more than five tons. Now paleontologists have uncovered a therizinosaur that stands out even among its unusual relatives—because it’s missing a finger. Illustration by Henry Sharpe By Asher Elbein Published October 7, 2026 Ever since the first well-preserved mosasaur skeletons were found in the late 1800s, paleontologists have recognized that these flippered sea lizards lived in the ocean. But their tails showed no sign of the specializations seen in sharks or dolphins, leading many to assume the marine reptiles sculled under the waves like giant crocodiles or eels. Because this serpentine swimming style creates a lot of drag underwater — especially at large sizes — researchers concluded that mosasaurs weren’t efficient swimmers. But in the 2010s, a reassessment of mosasaur anatomy suggested they had relatively stiff bodies, and one study showed that their tails ended in a shark-like tail fin. The harbour wall of Lyme Regis is also known as The Cobb. Thomas Faull, Getty Images By Jessica Prupas Published August 1, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Were you to dig below Lyme Regis’ bunting-slung streets, you’d hit a geological marvel: the Blue Lias. This vast sequence of limestone and shale layers, formed during the Mesozoic era some 200 million years ago, reveals fossils as it erodes, making the town one of Europe’s most important paleontological centres. It’s a badge locals wear proudly: you’ll find a weather-beaten statue of celebrated fossil hunter Mary Anning overlooking Church Cliff Beach. In 1823, while wandering Lyme Regis’s coastline, she unearthed the world’s first complete skeleton of a Plesiosaurus and, nearly two centuries after her death, the town remains a magnet for excavators. pages.text: Tracking a Mystery: When and How the First Americans Arrived | National Geographic The Oregon Coast, pictured here, may have been a byway for the first Americans as they followed the nutrient-rich coast southward on foot and by boat, says the new book, Atlas of a Lost World . Photograph by Ty Milford, Aurora BOOK TALK When, How Did the First Americans Arrive? It’s Complicated. The first Americans weren't one group of people; they arrived at different times, and likely by different methods. By Simon Worrall Published June 9, 2018 • 13 min read How did human beings first come to North America? Across the Bering Strait, on foot? Down the “kelp highway” by boat? Across the Atlantic via the polar ice cap? And when did they reach here? 10,000 years ago? 40,000? Or were they always here, as the Navajo and other Native American tribes believe? In his new book, Atlas Of A Lost World , author Craig Childs sets off to test these different theories on the ground, traveling from Alaska to Chile, Canada to Florida. What he finds, despite the best efforts of archaeologists and the latest technology , still remains in many ways a mystery. Speaking from his home in Colorado, he explains why many Native Americans reject the idea that their ancestors migrated from somewhere else; how an archaeologist nicknamed Dr. Poop believes he has identified the first human excrement in America ; and why diversity seems to have been built into America’s DNA. Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty Images Trump administration Trump administration planning to reimburse doctors treating vaccine ‘injury’ Experts warn that sweeping changes elevate health secretary RFK Jr’s anti-vaccine agenda and personal profit Melody Schreiber Sun 15 Nov 2026 07.00 EST Last modified on Sun 15 Nov 2026 07.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Trump administration is finalizing a rule to reimburse doctors who diagnose, treat and counsel patients with side effects from vaccines in what experts believe is an attempt to undermine trust in vaccines and to create an evidence base on their purported risks. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), also announced the creation of a vaccine “injury” research center at the National Institutes of Health and has sought to reshape the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) – actions that point to Kennedy’s longtime activism against vaccination as well as the profits he and his network have made from vaccine lawsuits. A red carpet was rolled out for Trump as he walked off Air Force One in Manila. A band played one of his favourite songs, Y.M.C.A., before he was whisked away by helicopter to a hotel. Trump's first meeting at the Asean Summit was with America's partners in the Quad - India's Narendra Modi, whom he described as a "very tough man", Japan's Sanae Takaichi, who "may be even tougher", and Australia's Anthony Albanese. "Our countries are the four corners of the free, open, stable, prosperous Indo-Pacific," the US president said. "We have outstanding relationships and co-ordinate closely... my phone is always open," Trump added. Many countries in South East Asia have been hit hard by Donald Trump's tariffs and his war on Iran - but their exports to the US rose 30% last year thanks to the AI boom for which the region manufactures many of the components. One year ago, EPA finalized a comprehensive set of organizational improvements that refocused its work on the agency’s core mission of providing clean air, land, and water for communities across the nation. These cross-agency shifts are expected to deliver more than $300 million annually for the American people.
